Zelano Lab · EEG-breathing · 260917_EEG_NWU_JW · recorded 2026-09-17

JW Paced Breathing RSA

Respiratory sinus arrhythmia (RSA, the swing of the RR interval inside each breath) as a function of breath length and inhale volume across about 69 minutes of paced breathing, and how the final 10 minutes of focused breathing compare with the paced period and with the opening 6 minutes of audiobook listening. Same analysis as the KG session two days earlier. One 85.3-minute recording made in two files (the acquisition was stopped for 56 s at 6.0 min); no event marks; the three periods are defined by time.

  • Breath length is again the dominant driver. Median RSA climbs from 38–52 ms at breaths under 4 s to 124–150 ms at 7.5–9 s and 156–214 ms at 9–11 s. Spearman ρ = 0.56 with log length and 0.35 with log inhale volume; peak-to-trough amplitude is unrelated to RSA in this participant (ρ = 0.006, p = 0.86), which is the clearest case yet for volume over amplitude as the depth measure.
  • Inhale volume is a real second factor here, not a minor one. Within every length bin with enough breaths the deepest tertile is above the shallowest (under 4 s: 38 → 41 → 52 ms; 4–5 s: 46 → 49 → 58; 5–6 s: 47 → 60 → 66; 6–7.5 s: 61 → 90 → 114; 7.5–9 s: 124 → 134 → 150). The length × volume interaction is large (+89 ± 8 ms per log² unit, p ≈ 10⁻²⁸; KG: +15): a doubling of volume is worth almost nothing at 3–4 s and 40–50 ms at 7–9 s. The fitted surface's contours run diagonally above 5 s.
  • The final 10 minutes are slower and shallower than the paced breathing yet carry more RSA (10.7 vs 12.7 breaths/min, inhale volume 93 k vs 118 k, RSA 82 vs 58 ms, p = 2·10⁻⁴), with a slightly lower heart rate (66.1 vs 67.2 bpm) and twice the multi-peaked breaths (59 % vs 31 %). Against the opening 6 minutes (natural breathing during the audiobook) RSA is 82 vs 52 ms at an unchanged heart rate.
  • Given their length and volume, the final-10 breaths carry about 28 ms more RSA than the paced breathing predicts — and that excess belongs to the ragged breaths. The local-linear surface fitted on paced breaths predicts 68 ms for them; observed is 97 ms (+28.5 ± 6.7 ms SEM, median +13.6, sign-rank p = 2·10⁻⁴, 71 of 94 breaths inside the paced support). Split by breath quality: the 22 single-peaked, regular final-10 breaths inside the support are +15 ± 9 ms (median +4, p = 0.20); the 49 multi-peaked or irregular ones are +35 ± 9 ms (median +16, p = 5·10⁻⁴). Matched on length, the difference is confined to 5–6 s breaths (99 vs 60 ms, p = 6·10⁻⁵), and within clean breaths it shrinks to 86 vs 60 ms (n = 10, p = 0.07).
  • Compared with KG: KG's final 10 minutes were deeper and steadier than the paced breathing and sat on the paced surface (+6 ms, n.s.); JW's are shallower, more ragged and sit above it, driven by breaths with several inspiratory efforts. Whether such breaths produce genuinely larger vagal swings or the segmentation attributes two efforts' worth of RR modulation to one breath cannot be separated from this recording alone.
  • Data quality is good: clean ECG at 67.2 bpm on the inverted lead-1 detector (5,733 beats), respiration polarity confirmed by the heartbeat (RR shortens 26 ms within 2 s of each inhale onset, 46 ms in the final 10 minutes), 94 % of breaths pass the breath QC, and the paced breathing was far less ragged than KG's (51 % of paced breaths clean vs 14 %). The two recording files were stitched end to end; the 5 breaths touching the seam are excluded.
What was done

From raw export to analysed session

  • Reorganised the participant folder to the standard layout: the Neuralynx export 2026-09-17_09-56-12 now sits in AtlasData\, with raw\ and preProc\ alongside.
  • Found that the acquisition had been stopped and restarted once: every channel exists as CSCn.ncs (09:56–10:21, 6.02 min) and CSCn_0001.ncs (10:21–11:41, 79.26 min, starting 55.6 s after the first file closed); the _0002 files are empty stubs. Probed the channels before writing the load script: same map as KG (EEG CSC33–64 with a 60-Hz fraction under 0.5 %, ECG CSC25/26/27 at ~67 bpm with lead 1 inverted, respiration CSC31 with CSC32 as an inverted near-duplicate kept as rsp2, photodiode CSC269 flat).
  • Wrote and ran LoadData_260917_EEG_NWU_JW.m, which reads both files and stitches them end to end (the lab's run-stitching convention, no gap samples inserted) and records the seam and the wall-clock gap in a segments table → raw\raw_pacedBreathing\raw_pacedBreathing.mat (1.14 GB).
  • Extended the pacedBreathing task so multi-file recordings travel through the pipeline: the seam positions are carried to the final at 500 Hz (outDat.segments) and every breath within 5 s of a seam is flagged (behDat.nearSeam); the shared core (resample to 500 Hz, EEG cleaning with blink ICA and Laplacian, the standard segmentBreaths_zlp segmentation with breathMetrics features, ECG beat detection 1,0,lt,-3.5 → RR-interval series, per-breath QC and RSA) is untouched. The pipeline's data-driven block segmentation (23 blocks) is stored but, as requested, not used to group anything here.
  • Ran the pipeline unattended on the lab desktop under the run-on-guess convention (outputs saved, parameters left as guess, every QC figure written), added row 337 to dataTracking.xlsx, exported the 50-Hz pack and built this summary with the session-agnostic batch\pacedBreathing_respHRV_summary.m (renamed from the KG script; period lengths are now settings). An independent four-lens code review with adversarial verification ran on the new stitching and seam code; its confirmed findings are fixed (see Quality checks).
Session overview

85.3 minutes, 970 breaths, three periods

First 6.0 minutes (the first recording file): audiobook, natural breathing at 11–14 breaths/min (80 breaths). 6.0–75.3 min: paced breathing (785 breaths) — about 7 minutes of instructions and practice at 12–17 breaths/min, then three descending sweeps of about 15 → 13 → 11 → 9 → 7 → 6 breaths/min (13.5–33.5, 33.5–53.5 and 53.5–75 min; the slow end of the third sweep was ragged and irregular). Last 10 minutes: focused breathing at 10.7 breaths/min (105 breaths). Each dot is one breath; grey dots failed the breath QC; the red dashed line is the seam between the two recording files.

Respiratory HRV vs breath length and inhale volume

RSA follows breath length, and inhale volume adds a lot at slow paces

RSA is the within-breath RR swing: maximum minus minimum RR interval between one inhale onset and the next (the pipeline's RR_max_min, in ms). Breath length is the inhale-to-inhale period. Depth is the breathMetrics inhale volume on the raw respiration trace (bm_inhaleVolumesRaw, raw units), split into tertiles across the paced breaths (cuts at 105 k and 130 k). Good-QC paced breaths only (n = 746); the final 10 minutes (n = 94 good breaths) are overlaid in violet with their mean.

Median RSA (ms) by length × inhale volume

Cells with fewer than 8 breaths are left blank. Colour is one blue ramp from 35 to 160 ms.

Coefficients are per natural-log unit of the predictor centred on its mean; multiply by 0.69 for the effect of a doubling. Intercept ≈ 67 ms = RSA at the mean paced breath. KG's corresponding additive coefficients were 62.5 (length) and 8.2 (volume) with R² 0.29 — the length effect is similar, the volume effect is three times larger here and the interaction six times larger.

The length × volume surface

A local-linear kernel regression (Gaussian kernel, bandwidth 0.35 SD in standardised log length / log volume) fitted on the 746 good paced breaths gives a model-free estimate of RSA at every combination of length and inhale volume the participant actually produced. Cells with too little paced support are blank.

Is the final-10-minute RSA more than the breathing pattern predicts?

The paced-breathing surface above is used as the predictor: each final-10 breath's length and inhale volume are looked up on the surface (a local-linear fit that never saw the final-10 data) and the observed RSA is compared with that prediction. The map shows the kernel-weighted mean error over the length × volume plane where final-10 breaths exist.

  • Ragged versus smooth breaths. The final-10 breaths inside the paced support split into 22 clean ones (one flow peak, local period CV under 0.20) and 49 ragged ones. The clean breaths are +15.0 ± 8.8 ms above the surface (median +4.3, sign-rank p = 0.20; the parametric additive model gives +7 ms, median +0.3, p = 0.68). The ragged breaths are +34.5 ± 8.8 ms above it (median +15.8, p = 5·10⁻⁴). Pooled over the whole final period, clean final-10 breaths have a median RSA of 59 ms against 53 ms for clean paced breaths (p = 0.08) and 55 ms for clean breaths in the first 6 minutes (p = 0.38); ragged final-10 breaths have 89 ms against 68 ms for ragged paced breaths (p = 0.03).
  • Matched breath length. 4–5 s: 52 vs 51 ms for paced breaths of the same length (n = 21 vs 232, p = 0.54). 5–6 s: 99 vs 60 ms (n = 33 vs 142, p = 6·10⁻⁵, δ = 0.45) although the final-10 breaths in that bin were shallower (96 k vs 120 k). 6–7.5 s: 86 vs 89 ms (n = 32 vs 80, p = 0.60). Restricted to clean breaths the 5–6 s contrast is 86 vs 60 ms (n = 10 vs 91, p = 0.07) and the 6–7.5 s contrast reverses (56 vs 82, n = 8 vs 38, p = 0.21).
  • Parametric check. The additive log-length + log-volume model fitted on the paced breaths predicts 69 ms on average for the final-10 breaths against 92 observed: +23.4 ± 5.5 ms, median +9.9 ms, sign-rank p = 5·10⁻⁴.
  • Sensitivity to the period boundary. Taking the opening period to 13.5 min instead (the start of the first clean pace sweep, so that instructions and practice count as natural breathing) leaves every conclusion in place: surface residual +28.1 ± 6.8 ms (median +12.8), additive +21.2 ± 5.6, final-10 RSA 82 vs 60 ms for the paced period (p = 0.001) and vs 51 ms for the opening period (p = 10⁻⁸).
  • Reading. Smooth focused breaths in the final 10 minutes carry roughly the RSA the paced surface predicts for their length and volume; the extra RSA of the period comes from breaths with two or more inspiratory efforts, which produce 20–35 ms more RR swing than smooth paced breaths of the same length and volume. Whether that reflects a real difference in vagal drive during multi-effort breaths or a bookkeeping effect (two efforts' worth of RR modulation credited to one breath) cannot be decided from this recording; comparing with the EEG or with a per-effort segmentation would be the next step.
Ragged and forced breathing

Paced breathing was mostly smooth; the focused breathing was not

Two per-breath regularity measures travel with every breath in the saved table: nSubPeaks, the number of local flow maxima inside the breath (prominence ≥ 15 % of the breath amplitude on a 100-ms smoothed trace), and localPeriodCV, the coefficient of variation of breath length over the ±3 surrounding breaths. A breath is clean when it passes the standard breath QC, has one flow peak and a local CV below 0.20.

Paced breaths with ≥ 2 flow peaks

59 %

Unlike KG (76 % multi-peaked paced breaths), this participant paced smoothly through the first two sweeps; raggedness appeared at the slow end of the third sweep (65–75 min, local CV 0.3–0.4) and persisted into the focused breathing, where more than half the breaths carry two or more flow peaks at a shallow volume. The regression is therefore repeated on the clean subset (same signs; a steeper length slope of 95 ms per log unit, R² 0.49), the final-10 comparisons are reported for clean and ragged breaths separately above, and the sub-peak count is stored per breath so ragged stretches can be dropped from a later analysis.

Quality checks and caveats

What was verified, and what still needs a human look

Verified

  • Respiration polarity. The inhale-locked RR interval falls by 26 ms within 1.8–2.1 s of every detected inhale onset in the opening and paced periods and by 46 ms in the final 10 minutes (figure below), the expected inspiratory acceleration, so inhale is positive (rspFlip = +1). The onset-locked respiration average rises after onset. (CSC32 is an inverted copy of CSC31 in this recording; the pipeline uses CSC31.)
  • ECG. 5,733 beats at 67.2 bpm from lead 1 with the inverted-R detector used across the 2026 rig; clean beat-detection window; no ECG fallback was triggered.
  • Breath detection. The shared segmentation engine found 970 breaths; 914 pass the breath QC (94 %; 95 % of paced breaths); the detected rate staircase matches the spectral dominant-frequency staircase of the raw channel.
  • Recording and stitching. Two 2 kHz files (722,432 + 9,510,912 samples) stitched end to end with the 55.6-s stop recorded in the segments table; 0.01 % dropped samples filled by interpolation; 5.07 GB export intact in AtlasData. Five breaths within 10 s of the seam are excluded from every statistic.
  • Independent review. A four-lens review (stitching, pipeline plumbing, summary generalisation, static analysis) with adversarial verification confirmed the stitching arithmetic, the 500-Hz seam positions (sample 180,609 = 6.02 min, exact) and the seam-flag logic, and found three things now fixed: the seam and period settings were being dropped from the stats JSON; a silent try/catch in the load script could leave the wall-clock gap as NaN (it did on the first run — the raw file was patched from the Neuralynx headers and the script now fails loudly); and a few figure labels still said "final 10 min" regardless of the setting. Its filter-transient analysis of the stitched step motivated the 10-s analysis-level exclusion around the seam.

To review

  • Period boundaries are by the clock, and the opening one is an assumption. The first period is taken as the first recording file (0–6.0 min), on the reading that the acquisition was stopped when the audiobook ended. The breathing after the restart stays at 12–17 breaths/min with natural-looking volume until the first clean pace sweep begins at about 13.5 min, so some or all of 6–13.5 min may be instructions and practice rather than paced breathing; it holds 13 % of the "paced" breaths and the sensitivity run above shows no conclusion depends on where the line is drawn. If the audiobook actually continued past the restart, rerun with ZLP_PRE_SEC set accordingly.
  • The final-10 excess rests on ragged breaths (see above): 59 % of the final-10 breaths are multi-peaked and only 27 % are clean. The clean-breath comparison is small (n = 22–28) and not significant.
  • Extrapolation. 23 of the 94 final-10 breaths lie outside the paced support (inhale volume below about 70 k); they are excluded from the surface residual but not from the period medians.
  • Inhale volume is in raw sensor units. Proportional to volume only if the sensor is linear in flow; fine for within-session comparisons, and not comparable in absolute terms across participants (KG's 90 k–190 k and JW's 90 k–120 k are on different belts and gains).
  • Parameters are still marked guess. Respiration channel, polarity, ECG detector and EEG settings were chosen from the channel probe and the cohort defaults; the run-on-guess QC figures (paramCheck_rsp, paramCheck_ECG, ECG_beatDetect, removedBlink) are in the figure folder. Promote the sheet row to curated once inspected.
  • EEG. The EEG stage ran to completion (blink ICA figure saved); channel-level EEG quality was not part of this summary. The stitched step passes through the 0.03-Hz high-pass, so EEG and respiration baselines are disturbed for a few seconds after 6.0 min.
  • RSA definition. Within-breath RR max − min is sensitive to breath length by construction; this is the intended physiological quantity here, but frequency-domain HRV would need its own analysis window.

Both participants show the same length-dominated RSA response and a volume effect that grows with breath length; JW's volume effect is larger. The focused breathing differs: KG breathed faster and deeper than the paced period and landed on the paced surface; JW breathed slower, shallower and more raggedly and landed above it, with the excess confined to multi-effort breaths.
